issue.title: Use-after-free in `bytearray` search methods via re-entrant `__index__`

labels.name: type-crash
labels.description: A hard crash of the interpreter, possibly with a core dump

issue.body:
### What happened?

`bytearray.index(x)` converts `x` to a single byte using index before performing the search.
A crafted `__index__` can call `bytearray.clear()`, freeing or resizing the buffer after `str` have been captured. The subsequent search (`stringlib_find_char`) then dereferences the stale pointer, resulting in a heap use-after-free.

Note that, this may share the same root cause as #142559 and #142558.

**Proof of Concept:**
```python
victim = bytearray(b'A' * 0x1)

class Evil:
    def __index__(self):
        victim.clear()
        return 65

victim.index(Evil())
```

**Vulnerable Code Snippet**

<details>

```c
static PyObject *
bytearray_index_impl(PyByteArrayObject *self, PyObject *sub,
                     Py_ssize_t start, Py_ssize_t end)
/*[clinic end generated code: output=067a1e78efc672a7 input=c37f177cfee19fe4]*/
{
    return _Py_bytes_index(PyByteArray_AS_STRING(self), PyByteArray_GET_SIZE(self),
                           sub, start, end);
}

PyObject *
_Py_bytes_index(const char *str, Py_ssize_t len, PyObject *sub,
                Py_ssize_t start, Py_ssize_t end)
{
    Py_ssize_t result = find_internal(str, len, "index", sub, start, end, +1);
    if (result == -2)
        return NULL;
    if (result == -1) {
        PyErr_SetString(PyExc_ValueError,
                        "subsection not found");
        return NULL;
    }
    return PyLong_FromSsize_t(result);
}

Py_LOCAL_INLINE(Py_ssize_t)
find_internal(const char *str, Py_ssize_t len,
              const char *function_name, PyObject *subobj,
              Py_ssize_t start, Py_ssize_t end,
              int dir)
{
    char byte;
    Py_buffer subbuf;
    const char *sub;
    Py_ssize_t sub_len;
    Py_ssize_t res;

    if (!parse_args_finds_byte(function_name, &subobj, &byte)) {
        return -2;
    }

    if (subobj) {
        if (PyObject_GetBuffer(subobj, &subbuf, PyBUF_SIMPLE) != 0)
            return -2;

        sub = subbuf.buf;
        sub_len = subbuf.len;
    }
    else {
        sub = &byte;
        sub_len = 1;
    }

    ADJUST_INDICES(start, end, len);
    if (end - start < sub_len)
        res = -1;
    else if (sub_len == 1) {
        if (dir > 0)
		    // Bug: *str has been freed already
            res = stringlib_find_char(
                str + start, end - start,
                *sub);
        else
            res = stringlib_rfind_char(
                str + start, end - start,
                *sub);
        if (res >= 0)
            res += start;
    }
    ...
}

Py_LOCAL_INLINE(int)
parse_args_finds_byte(const char *function_name, PyObject **subobj, char *byte)
{
    if (PyObject_CheckBuffer(*subobj)) {
        return 1;
    }

    if (!_PyIndex_Check(*subobj)) {
        PyErr_Format(PyExc_TypeError,
                     "argument should be integer or bytes-like object, "
                     "not '%.200s'",
                     Py_TYPE(*subobj)->tp_name);
        return 0;
    }
    
    // Implicitly call __index__ method that free the *subobj buffer
    Py_ssize_t ival = PyNumber_AsSsize_t(*subobj, NULL);
    if (ival == -1 && PyErr_Occurred()) {
        return 0;
    }
    if (ival < 0 || ival > 255) {
        PyErr_SetString(PyExc_ValueError, "byte must be in range(0, 256)");
        return 0;
    }

    *subobj = NULL;
    *byte = (char)ival;
    return 1;
}
```

</details>

comments.body:
@jackfromeast Thanks for the report! I think refactoring the code so that `find_internal` (and maybe `_Py_bytes_index`) does not take a python object `subobj` as argument but a plain index would resolve the issue. The `find_internal` is not used too often (and is internal). The `subobj` can also be a buffer object, so refactoring is not entirely trivial.

I will mark the two other issue reports as duplicates of this one.
We fixed a UAF in `__setitem__` but I forgot to check the other methods actually: #91153
The NEWS entry was in a wrong section. It should be in "Core and Builtins".

Thank you @jackfromeast for your detailed and helpful report. Please use `<details>` next time to collapse long lists and listings.

Thank you @fatelei and @cmaloney for your PRs.
